examples.question_text:
A council wants to know residents' opinions about a new park.
(a) It interviews only members of a local gardening club. Explain why this sample may be unrepresentative.
(b) It instead invites all residents to reply online, but only $36$ of $600$ residents reply. Explain why the replies alone may not represent all residents.
(c) It interviews only $3$ residents. Explain the problem with this sample.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Gardening club members may have different views about parks from other residents. The sample leaves out the views of residents outside the club.
(b) Residents who choose to reply may have different views from those who do not. Inviting everyone does not make the replies representative of everyone.
(c) Three residents may not cover the variety of opinions in the population.

examples.question_text:
A student plans a survey about a new school library.
(a) Explain a fault in: 'Do you agree that our wonderful new library is excellent?'
(b) The only response choices are 'Excellent', 'Good' and 'Satisfactory'. Explain a fault in these choices.
(c) Suggest more suitable wording and a response section.
(d) Explain a fault in: 'Do you visit the library and borrow books?'
(e) Write a suitable question to find out how long students spend reading.
examples.solution_text:
(a) 'Wonderful' and 'excellent' present the library positively and encourage a favourable answer. This is a leading question.
(b) There is no choice for a negative opinion. Students who are dissatisfied cannot give a suitable answer.
(c) Ask: 'How would you rate the new school library?'
Provide: Very good, Good, Neither good nor poor, Poor, Very poor, Have not used it.
(d) Visiting and borrowing are different actions. A student might visit without borrowing, so one answer cannot clearly describe both.
(e) Ask: 'How many hours did you spend reading outside lessons during the past seven days?' Allow a numerical answer, including zero.

examples.question_text:
(a) A school introduces a revision programme. The mean test mark increases from $11$ before the programme to $14$ afterwards. What other information would help show whether the programme caused the improvement?
(b) A study of delivery businesses includes only businesses still operating after five years. Explain why this may give a misleading picture of business success.
examples.solution_text:
(a) Compare the improvement with a comparable control group that did not use the programme. Use comparable tests over the same period and keep other relevant conditions the same. Marks might improve without the programme.
(b) Businesses that closed are excluded. Looking only at surviving businesses leaves out failures and can make success appear more common. This is survivorship bias.

examples.question_text: A survey asks: 'How often do you buy lunch?' The choices are 'Rarely', 'Sometimes' and 'Often'. Another question asks how long lunch takes, with choices '$0$–$10$ minutes', '$10$–$20$ minutes' and '$20$–$30$ minutes'. Explain the faults in the questions and response choices.
examples.solution_text:
The first question gives no time frame. Respondents may answer about different periods.
'Rarely', 'Sometimes' and 'Often' may mean different frequencies to different people.
The time intervals overlap at $10$ and $20$ minutes, so those answers fit two choices.
There is no choice for a lunch taking more than $30$ minutes.

examples.question_text:
A health centre mails questionnaires to $1200$ discharged patients about their experience. Only $90$ patients reply, and the centre reports their answers without following up the other patients.
Calculate the response rate and identify the data collection fault.
examples.solution_text:
Response rate $=\frac{90}{1200}\times100\%=7.5\%$.
The patients who replied may have different experiences from those who did not. Reporting only their answers without following up non-respondents leaves a risk of non-response bias. The low response rate alone does not prove the direction of any bias.

examples.derivation: 90 ÷ 1200 × 100% = 7.5%. The remaining 1110 patients did not reply.
